decision.explanation: Since sqrt(3-12x^2)=sqrt(3)sqrt(1-4x^2), an antiderivative is (sqrt(3)/2)arcsin(2x). Evaluating from -1/4 to 1/4 gives (sqrt(3)/2)(pi/6-(-pi/6))=sqrt(3)pi/6.

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-12{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3\cdot (1-4{x}^{2})}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(2x)}^{2}.$   

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-0.25$ | $0.25$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-0.5$ | $0.5$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-12{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.5}^{0.5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{\int }_{-0.5}^{0.5}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-0.5}^{0.5} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0.5)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-0.5)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $3x.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $3x.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So. let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So. let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{1+(2x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =10\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =5\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =5\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{6{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{6}}{|\sqrt{6}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{6}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{6}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{6}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{6{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{6}}{|\sqrt{6}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{6}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{6}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{6}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
